bottlenecks.reading: Scarce input is powered, connected data-center capacity for GPUs. NBIS contracted more than 2 GW of power (Feb 2026) against about 170 MW active at 2025-12-31, so growth depends on converting contracted power to live capacity; the 20-F also flags rising scrutiny of data-center electricity demand by US policymakers and utilities, and competition for sites.

Build-out is capital-bound: NBIS capex was $5.66B in Q2 2026 (against revenue of $0.58B) and it funds this with converts, equity, prefunded warrants, customer prepayments and, on 2026-10-22, a $3.5B 364-day Citi facility at Term SOFR+2.75%; management cites more than $40B of investment-grade long-term customer commitments as collateral for asset-backed financing. Funding cost and dilution are the constraint on speed.

Demand is evidenced by take-or-pay contracts, not logos: the Meta agreement (five years, about $2.88B initial order, payable irrespective of utilisation, tranches delivered Dec 2025 and Feb 2026) and a Microsoft contract are named in the 20-F; but most other customer engagements are short-term and NBIS says it has limited experience delivering large contracts. Competitor CoreWeave's remaining performance obligations rose from $60.7B (2025-12-31) to $103.7B (2026-06-30), showing the shortage of contracted AI capacity is sector-wide.

Hypothesis: as supply of GPU clouds expands and demand shifts toward inference, price per GPU-hour falls and differentiation moves up the stack (Token Factory, Inferize/Eigen AI/Clarifai tech), which the 20-F itself anticipates ('increasing competition may lead to further pressures on pricing'); no NBIS price-per-GPU-hour series was gathered.

Hypothesis: capacity adders are the named AI clouds (CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda), the hyperscalers (AWS, Google, Microsoft, Oracle) and state-sponsored AI infrastructure programmes (20-F); how long the shortage lasts is not evidenced by an independent industry source in this lane.

notes: fd NAMED COMPETITORS (20-F Item 3D and Item 4, pf_10k_20260430): core AI infrastructure: specialised AI clouds CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda (Lambda Labs); general purpose clouds Amazon AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle; national government AI infrastructure initiatives. Token Factory (inference): Fireworks AI and Together AI. Smaller units (Avride, TripleTen) face competition in their sectors but are not named. Note the filing is a 20-F (foreign private issuer), not a 10-K.

fd COMPETITOR CRWV (fd_cw_sec_facts): revenue $1,915M FY2024 -> $5,131M FY2025 (+168%); Q2 2026 $2,575M vs $1,212M Q2 2025 (+112%); operating income $324M FY2024, -$46M FY2025, -$49M Q2 2026 (margin about -1.9%); capex $10.3B FY2025 and $14.1B in H1 2026; RPO $103.7B at 2026-06-30. Growth is decelerating from a larger base while margins thinned as depreciation and interest scale. Derived percentages are mine from these reported values.

fd SHARE (fd_cw_sec_facts, nm_rel_q2_2026): Q2 2026 revenue NBIS $582.3M vs CoreWeave $2,575M, so NBIS is about 22.6% of CoreWeave's size (derived); NBIS grew 5.5x year on year (582.3 vs 105.1 in Q2 2025) against CoreWeave's 2.1x, so NBIS is closing the relative gap in revenue, from a much smaller base. NBIS operating margin Q2 2026 -30.2% (derived from -175.9/582.3) against CoreWeave -1.9%: NBIS is far less profitable at present. This is relative growth in reported revenue, not a measured market-share figure; no attributed third-party market-share source was found (gap).
fd SHARE hypothesis: Crusoe, Lambda, Oracle, AWS, Google and Azure AI revenue were not collected, so share against the full named set cannot be stated.

fd CAPACITY (pf_10k_20260430): about 170 MW active power at 2025-12-31 and more than 2 GW contracted as of Feb 2026; four data-center types (greenfield Finland and Missouri, brownfield, build-to-suit New Jersey, co-location in Kansas City, UK, Israel, France, Iceland).

fd FUNDING (fd_rel_20261022, dated 2026-10-22, citable from 2026-10-24): $3.5B senior secured Citi facility, 364-day maturity, Term SOFR+2.75% rising to a maximum 3.50%; management states more than $40B of investment-grade long-term contract commitments; this is management's statement, not independently verified.
